Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for Sri Lanka Women's response with the bat. A bit of football is going on in the English huddle near the ropes. Now then, the two umpires walk out to the middle, and the English players also scatter across the field to take their respective positions. Chamari Athapaththu and Hasini Perera are the two openers for Sri Lanka Women. And as usual, Lauren Bell will open the attack for England Women. Perera to face. Off we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Okay then, 254 is the figure Sri Lanka Women are tasked up to hunt down to register their first two points in this World Cup. It is going to be quite a grind for the Lankan ladies, given their over-reliance on Chamari Athapaththu with the bat. An interesting stat shows that deliveries bowled under 75 kph turned significantly more, suggesting that extra flight provided greater grip and spin on this slowish surface. This will make the likes of Ecclestone, Smith and Dean interested as each of these three bowlers operates in different trajectories. So, the mantra for England? Get the Lankan skipper out early to assert dominance in the game. Should be an interesting chase. Stay tuned.

England Women's TAMMY BEAUMONT is up for a chat with the broadcasters. She says the conditions changed throughout the innings. It skidded initially, and in the middle phase, it assisted the spinners. On Nat's innings, she doesn't feel any pressure and says she soaked up the pressure, which helped her to play her game in the end. Reckons she was trying to take the game on with the new ball but overall, she is happy with the total on the board.

Boundaries had completely dried up, and Sciver-Brunt appeared focused on preserving her wicket as batters kept falling at the other end. It made sense, as losing her at that stage would’ve left England staring at a modest total. But the skipper shifted gears brilliantly, reaching her century and finishing strong towards the backend, as England added 49 runs in the final five overs to post a respectable total. That acceleration in the final overs was a perfect display of how to pace the innings in ODI cricket, under pressure.

The control and squeeze were there from the bowlers, as they didn't concede a single boundary for around seven overs in that 21-30 over phase, but Sciver-Brunt looked unbothered by that and brought up her well-constructed fifty. However, she kept losing partners at the other end as Sri Lankan spinners continued to produce regular breakthroughs. And with Capsey too, gone, England Women slipped from 146/3 to 168/6, with Inoka Ranaweera the destructor in chief, who also picked up a double whammy. In that 31-40 over phase, England Women lost three wickets and could only add 34 runs, with Nat Sciver-Brunt stranded alone at one end.

There was just enough grip and drift on the surface to keep the batters cautious, but Heather Knight and skipper Nat Sciver-Brunt - the pair who rescued England against Bangladesh - once again steadied things after early setbacks. Sciver-Brunt, dropped on just 3, made Sri Lanka pay as the duo built a vital 60-run stand for the third wicket through smart strike rotation and confident footwork against spin. It wasn’t about power-hitting, but spending time in the middle did the job as runs flowed naturally. However, just when things were looking ominous for Sri Lanka, Inoka Ranaweera struck to end the partnership, triggering a brief slide.

A spin-heavy start set the tone as England were put in to bat first. The Sri Lankan bowlers maintained good control with disciplined lines and lengths, though any looseners were duly punished. A few sloppy moments in the field also let England off the hook early on. A mix-up sent Amy Jones back, while Tammy Beaumont’s promising start was halted by Sugandika Kumari, leaving things evenly balanced at 50/2 after the Powerplay.

Take a bow, Nat Sciver-Brunt. In adversity, she rose to the occasion and fought like a warrior, that too, single-handedly. Won't be any exaggeration to say that it was truly a one-woman show in Colombo. 125/3 in the first 25 overs, followed by 128/6 in the next 25, England Women have managed to post the highest first inning total at the R. Premadasa, in this World Cup so far. At one stage, it didn't even look like England would survive for all the allotted overs, and this score on the board will hurt the Sri Lankans a lot.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK. Just when things were looking really ominous for the Lankans, they managed to strike at the right time. First dismissing the dangerous Heather Knight and getting rid of Sophia Dunkley soon after, they haven't allowed the English women to run away with the score. In fact, 24.3 was the last occasion since the last boundary came for England. Blue skies are opening up just in time as we get ready for the national anthems. The match officials are in the middle, and they are followed by players from both teams. It will be of the home team first, followed by England's.

England’s SOPHIE ECCLESTONE chats with Natalie Germanos. She says it feels great to be back in Colombo and shares that the team is off to a good start in the tournament. Sophie feels nice seeing the side show resilience against Bangladesh in their last game. About the pitch, she cheekily adds that she expects a bit of turn. Talking about the bowling combinations, she highlights their strong spin attack with herself, Charlie Dean, and Linsey Smith, along with experienced spinner Sarah Glenn in the squad, who has an impressive bowling record.

PITCH REPORT - Pommie Mbangwa and Sana Mir are pitchside with their thoughts. Pommie begins by pointing that there is a threat of rain with 71 percent of humidity. About the dimensions, it is 56 meters and 63 meters on the squares, with 70 meters down the ground. Shares that there is still a bit of work going on the pitch. Sana Mir joins him and shares that this pitch has offered something for both batters and bowlers, but she feels that spinners will play a key role as they have taken 18 wickets this tournament. Stresses that they should target the 3-4 meter area. Reckons that with the rain coming in, batting second would be a better option.

The skipper of England Women, Nat Sciver-Brunt, says they would have batted first, as she feels it's a good surface to bat on and expects the surface to slow down as the game progresses. Informs that they are playing the same team. On Alice Capsey, Nat says she is a brilliant all-rounder. Also admits they are not blessed with many all-rounders in England but she is a champion cricketer.  Mentions they are not taking the opposition lightly as she feels the Lankans have some great spinners who can control the game well.

The captain of Sri Lanka Women, Chamari Athapaththu, says that she is very confident of her bowling unit as they have an experienced lineup. She points out that the conditions are good for the spinners. Believes that if they restrict England to around 240, they can chase it down. Shares that they have enjoyed the rest days and have trained hard on Friday. Admits that they have struggled with the batting in the middle overs and shares that they have worked really hard on it. Feels privileged to play in front of the home crowd. Informs they have made one change - Dewmi Vihanga comes in for Achini Kulasuriya.

Considerable cloudiness, along with some late showers, is what the forecast suggests for the day in Colombo. A light drizzle was reported in the morning, but for now, it’s not raining, which means toss might be on time. The sky remains overcast and is expected to stay that way throughout the day. Covers were placed on the field earlier due to the morning drizzle, but for now it is dry with blue skies and scattered clouds hovering over the stadium. Let's keep our fingers crossed that we get a complete game of cricket.

So what will be the mantra of success for both sides? For England, removing Chamari Athapaththu cheaply could expose the rest of Sri Lanka’s inconsistent batting lineup. For the hosts, exploiting England’s earlier struggles against spin will be key. But who, besides Athapaththu, can step up? That remains the big question. Sri Lanka will need more than individual brilliance if they hope to trouble an England side that has far more depth in both departments. Can Sri Lanka pull off a repeat of what they achieved in the 2013 World Cup, and break England’s current 10-match winning streak against the Lankans in ODIs? But much will depend on the weather, which, unfortunately, does look a bit dicey. All we can do is hope for the best. Stay tuned for the toss and the team updates.

For Sri Lanka, this marks their first home assignment in the tournament. Against India, they showed flashes of resilience, first with the ball and then with the bat, hinting at a team that is balanced but still seeking conviction. Left-arm spinner Inoka Ranaweera will once again take centre stage. In the opening match, she grabbed three wickets in a single over and finished with a four-for, a performance that set the tone. If the Khettarama track offers the turn that is expected, Ranaweera, along with Chamari Athapaththu and Sugandika Kumari, could prove a formidable challenge for any batter. Ultimately, though, the contest may hinge on whether Sri Lanka’s fragile batting order can withstand the firepower of England’s bowling unit.

England arrive in Colombo after playing their first two matches in Guwahati. New conditions, new plans, and plenty to adapt to. Their biggest strength? Bowling. In both games, they have kept the opposition under 200, even bundling South Africa out for just 69. The spin trio of Linsey Smith, Charlie Dean, and the ever-consistent Sophie Ecclestone has been the backbone of their success, and in Colombo, they are likely to be the key difference makers again. But with the bat, there are some serious issues that need to be ironed out. They will be assured that their vulnerability at the top order isn’t a recurring pattern and will come out stronger. Heather Knight and Nat Sciver-Brunt will once again be pivotal in stabilizing and fortifying the middle order against a spin-heavy Sri Lankan bowling unit.

Sri Lanka have had a tricky start to the tournament, with two matches yielding a loss and a washout. More concerningly, they will take the field since the curtain raiser, which was 11 days ago, as their previous clash against Australia, almost a week back, was washed out by rain. With limited opportunity to find rhythm and assess form, the hosts face a tough test against a side of England’s caliber. Nat Sciver-Brunt's side remains one of the two unbeaten teams in the tournament so far, though their win against Bangladesh was far from comfortable, coming dangerously close to slipping away. England Women have shown both their ruthless edge and their ability to grind out results when tested under pressure.

They say ‘a smooth sea never made a skilled sailor,’ and both teams will need all their skill and grit as we reach chapter twelve of the ICC Women’s World Cup 2025. We touch down once again in Colombo, where Sri Lanka Women will host the four-time world champions, England Women, in what promises to be an exciting and hard-fought contest. A warm welcome to everyone following our coverage. It is wonderful to have you all with us.
... MATCH DAY ...

‘Fortune favours the brave,’ said Virgil once, and how perfectly that fits to the Women’s World Cup 2025. Every game here feels like a gamble between courage and chaos. One moment you’re flying high, the next, you’re tumbling down the order. With every nation eyeing that glittering trophy, every run, every over, every decision matters. A battle is going on of belief, nerves, and unshakable will. As the tournament steams ahead, each team has now dipped its feet into the World Cup waters, where some waded gracefully, and others got pulled into the current. England Women? They’ve looked unstoppable so far, picking up two wins from two matches. Sri Lanka Women? They’ve had a stumble and a washout - one painful defeat to India and one frustrating rain escape against Australia. And now, it is time for the 12th match of the ICC Women’s Cricket World Cup at Colombo’s R. Premadasa Stadium - England vs Sri Lanka. A battle between the powerhouse and the passionate. Who bends first under pressure? Who rises when it matters most? Oh, this is going to be good. Let’s know about England first, and wow, what a juggernaut they’ve been! Two games, two wins, two completely different stories. They humiliated South Africa for just 69 in the opener, yes, 69, and then fought through a gritty chase against Bangladesh to win by 4 wickets. Can you ask for a better balance between domination and determination? Linsey Smith spun magic in the first game, while Heather Knight showed nerves of steel in the second. When experience and momentum walk hand in hand - that’s a dangerous combo! But wait - can anyone actually stop this English machine? Their bowling has been tighter than a drum. Ecclestone and Smith are bowling like artists painting nightmares for batters, and Charlie Dean has joined in with rhythm and control. The pacers - Bell and Sciver-Brunt - are bowling with swagger. But here’s the million-dollar question - what happens if their top order crumbles early? Against Bangladesh, it nearly did. Beaumont, Jones, and Dunkley all fell cheaply. England’s middle order needs to wake up before Sri Lanka’s spinners come knocking. Now shift the camera to Sri Lanka - they’re the true romantics of this sport! One day they stun the world, another day they break their own hearts. Their first match against India showed flashes of brilliance - Chamari Athapaththu’s fearless stroke play, Dilhari’s fighting knock, and Ranaweera’s magical four-wicket spell. But consistency? That’s their biggest enemy. Their second match getting washed out might’ve given them rest, but also rust. Can they now use the home crowd to their advantage? Can the Lankan roar in Colombo? Chamari is the name itself that brings electricity to the field. If she gets going, Sri Lanka can turn the tables around. But she needs her troops to rally around her - Samarawickrama, Nilakshika Silva, and Hasini Perera must step up. Their bowling is talented - Ranaweera’s spin, Kulasuriya’s pace, and Prabodhani’s variations can trouble anyone, but can they hold their nerves against England’s calm and class? That’s the big ‘IF’ looming over Sri Lanka’s campaign. So what’s expected to be cooked at the R. Premadasa surface? Oh, the pitch here can be a tricky little devil. It slows down under lights, grip for spinners, turn for the tweakers, and a bit of uneven bounce to spice things up. Spinners, come here with dreams. Expect Ecclestone and Ranaweera to steal the spotlight. The weather? Humid, sticky, and maybe a drizzle or two - just enough to make the ball sweat and tempers rise. Let’s spice it up - key battles! Heather Knight vs Inoka Ranaweera - patience versus persistence! Nat Sciver-Brunt vs Chamari Athapaththu - the all-round queens in a face-off! Tammy Beaumont vs Udeshika Prabodhani - experience against early swing! And Linsey Smith vs Harshitha Samarawickrama - a test of technique versus temptation. Whoever wins these duels could flip the script. So, who’s got the upper hand? On paper - easy! England. They’ve beaten Sri Lanka in 17 of their 20 ODIs, including a 2-0 series win when they last met. But cricket’s charm lies in its uncertainty. Sri Lanka, playing at home, might just find that magical spark. All it takes is one Chamari special, one Ranaweera spell, and suddenly, history could be rewritten. Will the English empire continue its march, or will the Lankans pull off a festival upset in Colombo? We shall find out. Bring your cheers and your chills!
